We need to make sure that, um, the governance of these processes achieve results because reproducing patterns of exclusion, environmental degradation, and inequality is not going to give the communities that sustainable development aspiration, and it really can undermine any benefits that can come in the short run. Therefore, we absolutely advocate from this experience to understand that For Indigenous communities, land or territory is not a resource. It's also a source of life, identity, and cultural continuity. Therefore, when we are discussing energy transition, it's very important to absolutely take into account the rights-based approach to make sure that we are not just thinking about today, but we are also creating a prospect that can sustain in the future. In Chile, the UN system has supported spaces for dialogue. This is a super important role that we play in countries, in many countries around the world, but I would say that in particular the trust that the UN provides by opening a table and bringing different stakeholders grounded on the rights of Indigenous Peoples has been essential to meaningful consultations, participation, consistent with international standards. I have to say that our Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights—
Maria José, can I please ask you to wrap up?

Absolutely. Thank you. So, maybe a couple of gaps and 3 lessons. So, there is one element that is very important. One thing is the standards and the other thing is the implementation. And the other element is how this agenda is not marginal but central to the development, sustainable development agenda. So, 3 lessons from Chile. First, participation is not optional, it's a right. And I think as a community we need to work together with the local and central government as well as with the communities to realize it. Second, policy coherence is not a technical element, but it requires political commitment across institutions and sectors. Thank you. Thank you so much. Good morning, good afternoon. I'm going to start this. Bonjour. Dear Karima, I will be brief. Ambassadors, great to be here. My dear colleagues from the Interagency Group, I will invite you for a quick trip to the Philippines after listening to this very inspiring speech from Rey, this young, young, amazing activist. And I would like to bring you to the south, to Mindanao, where, you know, there has been a conflict for decades that has cost so many lives, more than 100,000 dead and so much suffering. And there has been a peace agreement 10 years ago, and since then there's an interim government working there, and we hope to will have elections now in September. And in this region, we're trying to bring the whole of UN approach to the work of the local authority in coordination with the national authority. And for us, the human rights approach is the framework in which we operate and we function. Actually, it's part and it's It's written in our cooperation framework and it's there also in our work too. I will give you just two quick examples from BARMM, from the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, two recent experiences where we brought the human rights lenses and approach. The first one is the approval last year of the Bangsamoro Labour and Employment Code. It was approved in 2025, supported by ILO and the whole UN system, and it's not just a new labour law, it's really a development instrument, a peace-building instrument, and a rights instrument. And it sets the standards for employment, workers' welfare, dispute resolution, and gave stronger mandatory to the Ministry of Labour and Employment on recruitment, on minimum wages, workplace safety, labour disputes, and so on and so forth. I mean, it's a very modern labour code that was approved for the first time in this region. And why does it matter? Because decent work is not only about job, it's about dignity, protection, social justice, trust in the institution, in a region emerging from decades of conflict, where labor rights are part of really, really building and sustaining peace. And so I will leave it there as a very strong and recent example of how we put human rights approach to sustainable peace. The second example, also in Barm, I thought was really interesting, but it's also really recent. For the first time, we have a landmark law that was supported by UNHCR, but the whole team, the Rights of Internally Displaced Persons Act in Barmes, so the IDP Law, as we called it. It was a landmark law, not only because it was approved by Barmes, in Barmes, but by the local government and Congress, but also because it's the first IDP law in Southeast Asia. So it's really an inspiring agreement. And it's very significant because displacement has been a recurring reality in the region, obviously caused by conflict, clan violence, disasters, climate-related shocks. And now the parliament described it as the first law in the Philippines specifically aimed at protecting the rights of internally displaced persons, and it's entered into force now. So again, the human rights-based approach is very concrete, and it means IDPs should not be only seen as beneficiaries of aid; they are rights holders, and they have the right to protection without discrimination, 'adéquate assistance', to information, to participation in decisions affecting them, and to durable solutions, whether return, local integration, resettlement. And this law creates a very strong basis for data, coordination, and accountability, so that displacement is just not managed as an emergency, but addressed as a development and governance challenge. So I just wanted to bring those two those two examples. Can I add another minute or not? Half a minute. I mean, I don't want to— I had some lessons learned, but maybe one key lesson learned for us is how powerful the human rights approach is when we connect it with our development agenda. And the SDGs and connected for all kinds of population, leaving no one behind. And in that case, with the labour code and the IDPs, we see how we can put it in action in creating the legal frameworks that will then help design more efficient public policies and have human rights really at the core of the development agenda. It's been a journey for us as country team with those lead agencies, but the whole country team reflecting how we can come together around those two pillar new laws and also inspiring also at national level where we still are working and advocating for a national IDP law, for instance. And there is no one in Bahr, but not yet. Approved at national level, so also showing how local work also can inspire national transformation with a human rights lens. I will leave it here. Thank you so much.

Thank you, Chair, Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. It's a great pleasure to take part in this important exchange. Let me first share with your— with you a conviction widely held by national human rights institutions. First, it's we will not achieve the Sustainable Development Goals nor respond effectively to environmental and climate change if human rights continue to be ignored in development processes. These convictions have been built greatly through the experiences of human rights actors, including national human rights institutions. Since the adoption of The 2030 Agenda, GANRI and its regional network have mobilized to promote human rights-based approach to implement the SDGs. The Merida Declaration adopted in 2015 marked an important step by recognizing the essential role and the key role of national institutions in monitoring, evaluating and implementing sustainable development commitments. Since then, national institutions have broadened their field of interventions and developed new approaches to their work. Yet, this evolution was not self-evident. Environmental and climate issues remained are relatively new for many national institutions which had traditionally focused on fundamental freedoms. Today, national institutions are fully engaged in these emerging challenges which require new skills, new tools, and new forms of cooperation. The experience of Network of National Institutions Institution in the Americas in relation of the Escazú Agreement illustrates this dynamic very well. It highlights, among other priorities, the need to protect also environmental human rights defenders who remain particularly exposed in many regions. GENRI, ladies and gentlemen, has developed several spaces for peer-to-peer cooperation, helping institutions to share experiences and build common responses to challenges that extend beyond the national borders. The growing engagement of regional and national institutions, as well as their active participation Participation in the Conferences of the Parties on climate change reflects a collective awareness: human rights and environmental justice and sustainable development are inseparable and form parts of the same protection and promotion agenda. This evolution is often more difficult in, in context of crisis, instability, or conflict, where immediate security and governance imperatives tend to push environmental concern into the background. Innovation for the SDGs cannot be reduced to technological advance only. It also means imagine new forms of governance, citizen participation, public policy monitoring, and institutional cooperation. Allow me to highlight two major challenges facing the national institutions. First concerns equitable access to innovation and to the benefits it generated. Second, concern the ability to ensure that the innovation being implemented effectively strengthen the protection and enjoyment of human rights. Our environmental and climate challenge— challenges make these requirements even more urgent.— in these contexts that innovation tools take on their full importance. In this regard, I welcome the tripartite partnership between UNDP, the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, and GANRYU. This cooperation has unveiled several concrete initiatives, including the development of the toolkit, a methodological guide to support national institutions in monitoring the rights to a clean, healthy, and sustainable environment. This tool represents an important step for the national institutions to strengthen their capacities and in data collection analysis public policy monitoring and identification of the most vulnerable populations. It also contributes to the better integration of human rights into national SDGs monitoring mechanisms. The growing engagement of national institutions in climate and environmental issues reflects a positive and the progressive dynamic. For Ghanai, innovation also lies in our collective ability to build strong partnership. Thus, our common challenge is to make innovation a true instrument, one that protects the most vulnerable, reduces inequalities, and strengthens environmental justice. Thank you.

Thank you, Madam Moderator. I hope I can do justice to this, but just to also acknowledge all the excellencies that have spoken before me, and especially Madam Maria Torres, who was actually at the helm of the Spotlight Initiative when we started in Malawi. Some years ago. Malawi is an example of that, and perhaps I would wish to state that Malawi has demonstrated how human rights evidence-based approaches can translate into concrete SDG results, and basically, especially for those furthest behind. With our hub that was developed, I would say that it's obviously flagship innovation, the Observatory Hub, and so far we've seen it has been able to capture, track, and analyze GBV cases in real time. Particularly the system has operated from the community district level to national level, ensuring that, you know, data of girls and women has been put into national decision-making. So it directly addresses the structural invisibility of violence and action across all levels for government. So, for example, the NHRI, we rely on that data to do our systemic violations— I mean, to do our systemic investigations of the violations that are coming out. So over 17,000 cases have been tracked and approximately 70% have reached prosecution and case completion, which is a great result. And it has also been operationalized from multiple districts, meaning that it's expanding and has got national replicability. Of course, there are challenges, as you rightfully point out, challenges to to do with data quality and sometimes institutional capacity, as well as the fact that when cases are tracked end-to-end, countries like Malawi, where internet is not free, that can be a challenge, particularly in terms of compiling and coordinating the data into the systems. So, capturing the data can be challenging. However, I would want to say that when we look at what has collected, this directly supports the elimination of violence against women and obviously addressing the issues of ending harmful cultural practices, so supporting SDG 5, 2, and 3. But then again, also, I think the HAB has helped us to integrate the data into development plans. So recently, the new administration that just came up in 2025 has announced that it would like to give money, transfer the money to the district assemblies through what is known as the Constituency Development Fund. So in this regard, it means there is also ownership by the national government to make sure that they are translating what is happening on the ground into national— national development plans. I would say that in terms of innovation, recognition, and replicability, The hub has also received recognition as a top digital development initiative for Malawi, which again puts us also on the global map, because it's designed to scale up the architecture, but also the national ownership, which is given to the National Statistics Office. And NHRI are able to access this data. This is not a pilot. It is a nationally owned system with global relevance., and the potential to be adapted by other member states for those that do not have it. And in closing, I would say that systems matter, so transformative change happens indeed when human rights principles are embedded into national systems, just as we've seen in Malawi, not just as standalone projects. But again, disaggregated data that is collected in real time can be one of the most powerful tools to have to advance accountability. Sustainability and equity, just as NHRI are well positioned to do that in the country. But also, I would also wish to add that sustained progress depends on integrated UN support. This would not have happened had it not been there was no UN support, particularly the support coming from UNDP, which has been very instrumental in systems building, but also in capacitating national human rights institutions. In that regard, they've shown leadership, and multi-sector— that multi-sector— multi-sector holder relationship and collaboration is very key. Thank you very much.

Thank you very much, Moderator. I'm Khalid Ramli. I'm representing the Moroccan National Human Rights Council. This engagement is especially relevant in the African context, where climate change disproportionately affects vulnerable communities, exacerbates inequalities, threatens livelihoods, food security, and access to water, and increases the risks of displacement and social instability. And I think this is also the reality, and perhaps trying to find a balance between being too pushy and disruptive protecting that trust that we try to build, but also making sure that we are, at least from the side of the UN, that those rights are non-negotiable and that we need to make sure that those two converge and the mindset shift that is needed at government and other institutions needs to happen. Development without rights is fragile. It is not something that stands and withstands the shocks, and we We are seeing it in many, many, many places, too many places to really doubt that. Today, what we've heard is definitely embedding human rights in development, whether we're talking about indigenous communities in lithium mines or whether we're talking about the southern parts of Philippines or other parts of the world. Participation is not a box to tick. It is really an approach, and it is a right as well. So making sure that, you know, women, young people, persons with disabilities, Indigenous communities, and other marginalized groups, IDPs or other, are at the very core and are not just there because we need to take pictures with them, but are there because their rights matter. Today's challenges—climate, fiscal pressures, gender equality, violence against women, critical minerals—they don't respect international institutional boundaries, and our responses should also be the same.
